paragraphs: The centroid’s two-to-one ratio applies to medians. A cevian through an arbitrary side point is not a median. For general intersections, use consistent masses, repeated area ratios, or affine coordinates. Each is a representation of the same linear balance along segments.

In a mass model, masses at two endpoints are inversely proportional to the distances to their balance point. Choose endpoint masses satisfying every given side ratio, then add masses at a combined point. Only after the system is consistent should you read off the desired distance ratio.

Coordinate parameters provide an independent check. A point written as A+t(D-A) has AP/AD=t and AP/PD=t/(1-t). The distinction between these ratios matters: a correct intersection calculation can still answer the wrong question. A point’s distance from the opposite base also changes linearly with t.

sections.title: Chain similarities and handle external points
paragraphs: Diagonals of a trapezoid create two similar triangles at the parallel bases. Their height ratio equals the base-length ratio, and their heights add to the trapezoid’s height. This locates the intersection without knowing the sloping sides. A parallel cross-section there can then be obtained by linear interpolation.

Lengths attached to similar figures, such as inradii, altitudes, and medians, scale by the ordinary length factor. Areas scale by its square. A partition into similar triangles can therefore make radii add to a multiple larger than the original radius even though the areas still add exactly.

Concurrent cevians and a collinear transversal use different ratio theorems. For an external intersection, sketch the point order and preserve the cyclic ratio orientation in Menelaus’s theorem. A positive-length formula needs the correct external configuration; a signed-coordinate calculation can verify both the ratio and the location.

derivation: Use K=bh/2 to derive common-base and common-height comparisons.
Scale both base and height to derive the square law for similar areas.
Write a cevian point as A+t(D-A) and distinguish t from t/(1-t).
pitfall: A length ratio, an area ratio, and a part-to-whole fraction are different quantities. Label the numerator and denominator before simplifying.

examples.stem: D is the midpoint of BC and E lies on CA with CE:EA=1:2. Lines AD and BE meet at P. Find AP/PD.
optionRationales: Use the whole side ratio on CA without balancing BC.
Reverse the ratio.
Treat both lines as medians.
Correct: Build consistent masses and translate back to a requested distance ratio.
Report AP/AD.
solution: Equal masses at B and C balance D. Choose B=C=2 so that CE:EA=1:2 is balanced by A=1.
The total mass at D is 4. Balancing A and D places P with AP:PD=4:1.
This is also an area argument: equal bases on BC give equal subareas, and the ratio on CA fixes the remaining height ratio.
A coordinate check uses A=(0,0),B=(1,0),C=(0,1); the intersection is (2/5,2/5), four fifths of the way along AD.
hints: Make the masses at B and C equal.
Choose the mass at A to satisfy the second ratio.
examples.misconception: Treat both lines as medians.
examples.decision: Build consistent masses and translate back to a requested distance ratio.

examples.stem: Two similar triangles have areas 18 and 50. Their corresponding altitudes differ by 8. Find the smaller altitude.
optionRationales: Report the larger altitude.
Use the area ratio directly for the altitudes.
Use the difference as the smaller height.
Assume the larger area doubles the height.
Correct: Combine similarity scaling with an additive length constraint.
solution: The area ratio is 9:25, so the positive length ratio is 3:5.
Write the altitudes as 3k and 5k. Their difference gives 2k=8.
Thus k=4 and the smaller altitude is 12.
Checking the two heights 12 and 20 gives squared ratio 144:400=18:50. This separates area scaling from the additive condition on lengths.
hints: Take the square root of the area ratio.
Represent both altitudes using a single scale parameter.
examples.misconception: Use the area ratio directly for the altitudes.
examples.decision: Combine similarity scaling with an additive length constraint.

verification.method: Solve the two independent linear constraints.

activity.prompt: D lies on BC with BD:DC=2:1. If P lies on AD with AP:PD=3:2, find [BPC]/[ABC]. Which given ratio is unnecessary?
activity.answer: The area ratio is 2/5; BD:DC is unnecessary.
steps: The triangles share base BC, so compare their perpendicular heights.
The height fraction is PD/AD=2/(3+2). The position of D along BC does not change this.

title: Circles: power, cyclic structure & tangents
summary: A circle problem often becomes short after you identify which invariant is available: an angle subtending a fixed arc, a power product from a fixed point, or equal tangent lengths.
objectives: Choose correct power factors and sign conventions.
Use center and tangent constructions only when they add useful relations.
Combine cyclic, area, and equal-tangent identities with feasibility checks.
teaching: A circle problem often becomes short after you identify which invariant is available: an angle subtending a fixed arc, a power product from a fixed point, or equal tangent lengths. These are different tools, and the location of the point determines which lengths and signs belong in the relation.
Draw the center only when its radii create useful perpendiculars or distances. Many cyclic-quadrilateral problems are better solved through angles and diagonals without introducing the center at all.

sections.title: Power is measured from one point
paragraphs: For an external point and a secant, the power product uses the distance to the near intersection times the distance to the far intersection. The internal chord length alone is not one of those factors. If the external segment is x and the internal part is y, the product is x(x+y).

A tangent is the limiting case with equal intersection distances, giving the square of its length. For an interior intersection of chords, the product of the two positive segment lengths equals R²-OP². The signed power OP²-R² is negative inside; state which convention you are using.

The chord-product theorem follows from similar triangles formed by joining opposite chord endpoints. Equal inscribed angles provide the correspondence. This proof explains why all four lengths must be measured from the same intersection point and why changing only one factor to a full chord breaks the relation.

sections.title: Use the center when it creates perpendiculars
paragraphs: A radius to a tangent point is perpendicular to the tangent. The perpendicular from a center to a chord bisects the chord. These facts turn tangent and chord lengths into right-triangle calculations, but the hypotenuse must be the radius or center-to-external-point distance in the correct triangle.

For intersecting circles, subtracting their coordinate equations cancels the quadratic terms and locates the common chord on a line perpendicular to the centers. Unequal radii generally put that line away from the midpoint of the center segment. Once its location is known, one radius triangle gives the half-chord.

For a common external tangent, parallel radii leave an offset equal to the difference of radii. Together with the center distance and the tangent segment, this forms a right triangle. An internal common tangent uses a sum instead; the drawing must establish which configuration occurs.

sections.title: Cyclic and tangent polygons combine local relations
paragraphs: An inscribed angle intercepts the arc not containing its vertex. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary. Ptolemy then relates the product of diagonals to the sum of opposite-side products. Check that supplied side and diagonal data describe a possible figure before using an algebraic identity.

Brahmagupta’s area formula applies to a cyclic quadrilateral, not an arbitrary quadrilateral with the same four sides. One derivation splits along a diagonal, uses the supplementary opposite angles, and eliminates the shared angle from the two triangle-area relations. The cyclic condition is the constraint that makes the four sides sufficient.

For an incircle, tangent segments from each vertex are equal. Their three pairwise sums recover the side lengths and show that a contact segment is the semiperimeter minus the opposite side. Joining the incenter to all vertices gives K=rs. Combining these two relations can recover an area without solving every side individually.

derivation: Use inscribed angles to prove the similar triangles behind chord power.
Draw a tangent radius to derive PT²=OP²-R².
Partition a triangle into three inradius-height triangles to derive K=rs.
pitfall: For a secant, outside times whole is the power product. Outside times inside generally gives the wrong equation even when every length is positive.

examples.stem: A tangent from an external point P has length 12. A secant meets the circle at A,B with PA=8. Find AB.
optionRationales: Report the whole secant.
Correct: Derive and correctly interpret tangent–secant power.
Use the tangent length instead of its square.
Confuse external and internal lengths.
Subtract PA from the tangent.
solution: Join the tangent point to the secant intersections. The tangent-chord angle relation produces two similar triangles and hence PT²=PA·PB.
Thus PB=144/8=18. This is the distance from P to the far intersection, not the length inside the circle.
The internal chord segment is AB=PB-PA=10.
Check the original power: 8(8+10)=144=12². Labeling the three secant lengths prevents an otherwise convincing wrong answer.
hints: Use tangent power and the whole secant length.
Subtract the external portion only after finding the whole.
examples.misconception: Report the whole secant.
examples.decision: Derive and correctly interpret tangent–secant power.

examples.stem: A triangle has sides 5,12,13. Find the distance between its incenter and the vertex opposite the side of length 13.
optionRationales: Use an unrelated side as a squared distance.
Add two perpendicular distances.
Report the inradius only.
Correct: Distinguish incenter and circumcenter through a local construction.
Use the circumradius.
solution: The side lengths satisfy 5²+12²=13², so the specified vertex is the right-angle vertex.
The area is 30 and the semiperimeter is 15, giving inradius two.
Place the legs on the coordinate axes. The incenter is (2,2), so the required distance is 2√2.
This uses the side data twice: first to recognize the right angle, then to obtain the radius. The circle’s center is not halfway along the hypotenuse; that would be the circumcenter.
hints: Recognize the triangle before choosing a circle formula.
An incenter is equally far from the two perpendicular legs.
examples.misconception: Report the inradius only.
examples.decision: Distinguish incenter and circumcenter through a local construction.

activity.prompt: An external secant has outside length 5 and inside length 15. Another secant from the same point has outside length 4. Find its inside length.
steps: The first power is 5(5+15)=100.
The second whole length is 100/4=25, so its inside length is 25-4=21.

title: Coordinates, transformations & lattice geometry
summary: Coordinates are a representation choice, not a command to expand every distance.
objectives: Choose coordinates that simplify geometry before calculating.
Use signed determinants and lattice gcds with correct boundary conventions.
Compose transformations and enforce geometric constraints on algebraic solutions.
teaching: Coordinates are a representation choice, not a command to expand every distance. Put a useful side on an axis, exploit a diagonal or midpoint, and look for cancellations before solving for all unknowns. A well-chosen coordinate system can turn an angle-free geometry problem into linear algebra with two variables.

Lattice problems add an integer structure to the picture. Primitive directions, determinants, and boundary gcds connect geometry with number theory; the continuous area and the discrete point count must be kept distinct.

sections.title: Choose a coordinate system that removes work
paragraphs: Translations and rotations preserve distances and areas, so place a convenient vertex at the origin and a side on an axis. A rectangle then has only two unknown dimensions. Squared-distance differences often cancel the quadratic terms, leaving linear equations for an unknown point or a relation independent of the point.

An equidistance condition describes a perpendicular bisector. Expanding squared distances is useful because the same x²+y² occurs on both sides. For several conditions, solve the resulting linear system before taking any square roots.

A diagonal can determine a square’s area without locating the other vertices. A midpoint construction can determine a quadrilateral’s area fraction without determining every side. Coordinate work is most effective when it preserves such geometric structure rather than replacing it with an unnecessarily large system.

sections.title: Determinants measure signed area
paragraphs: With one triangle vertex at the origin and edge vectors (a,b),(c,d), the signed parallelogram area is ad-bc; the triangle area is half its absolute value. The sign records orientation. A fixed positive area therefore usually produces two parallel linear loci, one on each side of a fixed base.

For a polygon, sum consecutive cross products in boundary order and close the final edge. Reordering vertices arbitrarily can create a crossed figure and change the signed sum. Use the absolute value only after the signed contributions have been combined.

An area maximum can become a one-variable quadratic after a line constraint eliminates a coordinate. Completing the square provides a bound and an equality point. Check that this point lies in the permitted region; an unconstrained algebraic maximum does not automatically solve a constrained geometry problem.

sections.title: Track integer and transformation structure
paragraphs: A segment with integer displacement (u,v) has gcd(|u|,|v|) primitive intervals. It has one more lattice point if both endpoints are included and one fewer if both are excluded. On a closed polygon, summing the interval counts counts each boundary lattice point once.

Pick’s theorem states K=I+B/2-1 for a simple lattice polygon. Compute the geometric area and the boundary count separately, then solve for the interior count. For a small example, verify by direct strict inequalities; this helps expose boundary points accidentally included as interior.

For transformations, write each coordinate rule and apply them in the specified order. A rotation about a nonorigin center requires translating to that center and back. Two transformations with familiar individual effects can compose to a different center or orientation. A fixed-point calculation provides a useful independent check of the final map.

derivation: Translate one triangle vertex to the origin and derive area from a parallelogram determinant.
Reduce an integer direction by its gcd to count primitive intervals.
Translate to a rotation center, apply the origin rotation, and translate back.
pitfall: A coordinate difference is not necessarily a perpendicular height. Use a determinant or establish perpendicularity before multiplying lengths for area.

examples.stem: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1,1),(7,3),(2,6).
optionRationales: Correct: Choose coordinates that simplify an area calculation.
Forget to halve the determinant.
Drop one signed cross term.
Halve twice.
Use coordinate differences as perpendicular legs.
solution: Translate the first vertex to the origin. The two edge vectors become (6,2) and (1,5).
The determinant 6·5-2·1=28 is the signed area of their parallelogram.
The triangle occupies half that area, so its area is 14.
Translation preserves area and simplifies the computation. An independent bounding-box decomposition removes the three surrounding right triangles from a 6×5 rectangle.
hints: Translate one vertex to the origin.
Use a determinant rather than treating oblique edges as perpendicular.
examples.misconception: Forget to halve the determinant.
examples.decision: Choose coordinates that simplify an area calculation.

examples.stem: How many lattice points lie on the boundary of the triangle (0,0),(6,0),(2,4)?
optionRationales: Correct: Explain the boundary gcd count without double-counting vertices.
Assume every integer x gives a point on each sloping side.
Miss one primitive step on the diagonal edge.
Exclude all vertices.
Count each vertex on two edges.
solution: The horizontal edge has six primitive intervals. The sloping edges have gcd(4,4)=4 and gcd(2,4)=2 primitive intervals.
For a closed polygon, summing interval counts gives boundary points because each vertex is the end of one interval and the beginning of another.
The boundary count is 6+4+2=12.
Alternatively, count 7+5+3 points on the three closed edges and subtract the three vertices counted twice. The same twelve points result.
hints: Find the primitive step on each edge.
Correct for shared vertices if counting closed-edge points.
examples.misconception: Count each vertex on two edges.
examples.decision: Explain the boundary gcd count without double-counting vertices.

verification.method: Independent union of lattice points on the three segments.

activity.prompt: For the triangle (0,0),(10,0),(4,6), compute its boundary lattice count and then its interior lattice count.
steps: The edge contributions are gcd(10,0)=10, gcd(6,6)=6, and gcd(4,6)=2.
The area is 30, so I=30-18/2+1=22.

title: Spatial geometry: nets, sections & volume
summary: A solid can be studied through a plane section, a flat net, or a volume comparison.
objectives: Choose between unfolding, cross-sections, and volume models.
Measure oblique sections and perpendicular heights correctly.
Use similarity and equality cases to solve spatial comparisons and maxima.
teaching: A solid can be studied through a plane section, a flat net, or a volume comparison. Choose the model that preserves the quantity asked for. A surface distance is preserved by unfolding; a volume can be compared through cross-sections; an oblique section needs its actual three-dimensional edge lengths.

The apparent difficulty often comes from looking at the wrong two-dimensional picture. A projection may shorten a segment, while a net preserves it. State which representation you are using before reading lengths from it.

sections.title: Separate interior, surface, and edge paths
paragraphs: A box’s space diagonal uses all three squared dimensions and passes through the interior. An edge path adds edge lengths. A shortest surface path generally does neither: unfold the crossed faces and use a straight segment in the resulting plane.

For opposite corners of a rectangular box, compare the three basic unfoldings obtained by combining two dimensions and retaining the third. Check that the segment remains within the unfolded faces. A candidate drawn across a gap or an extension of a face is not a permissible route.

Coordinates are also useful for classifying spatial configurations. Edge midpoints have one coordinate fixed at one half. Distinguishing parallel and nonparallel edge pairs gives a complete maximum-distance argument without checking every pair by hand.

sections.title: Construct the section before measuring it
paragraphs: A plane section’s vertices occur where the plane meets the solid’s edges. Solve these intersections first, then determine their cyclic order. For a symmetric cube section, the six vertices can reveal a regular hexagon, but its side is often a face diagonal fragment rather than the visible coordinate difference.

A regular pyramid’s altitude reaches the center of its base. Find the base center-to-vertex distance in the base plane, then use a spatial right triangle with a sloping edge. A slant height, an edge, and a perpendicular height are distinct lengths.

For a frustum, extend the sides to the original vertex and recover two similar cones or pyramids. Similarity relates both radii and heights. Subtract the two full volumes; averaging the two base areas without a derivation generally omits the necessary middle term.

sections.title: Volume comparisons retain structure
paragraphs: If lengths scale by k, areas scale by k² and volumes by k³. A parallel cut creates a small similar solid at the vertex; the remaining frustum is not itself similar to the original. Apply scaling to the small solid and subtract its volume afterward.

Displacement preserves volume. A fully submerged object raises water in a cylinder by its volume divided by the cylinder’s cross-sectional area. Check that the stated depth and container allow the assumed submersion and that no spilling changes the volume balance.

Cavalieri’s principle compares solids with equal cross-sectional areas at every height. In the drilled-sphere problem, each annular section matches a disk of a smaller sphere. This avoids an incorrect subtraction of a full cylinder that ignores the removed caps. For optimization, similarity can express an inscribed solid’s dimensions with one parameter; an inequality then gives a bound and an attainable equality configuration.

derivation: Unfold face distances without changing lengths inside each face.
Use base-center geometry and a spatial right triangle to derive a pyramid altitude.
Multiply an area scale by a height scale to derive cubic volume scaling.
pitfall: A projected segment, a surface path, and a straight distance through a solid are different objects. The shortest path must stay in the allowed region.

examples.stem: Find the shortest surface path between opposite vertices of a cube of edge 2.
optionRationales: Use the interior space diagonal.
Correct: Explain a feasible unfolding model.
Restrict travel to edges.
Ignore one unfolded dimension.
Use an unnecessarily long net.
solution: Unfold two adjacent faces into a rectangle with sides four and two. Opposite cube vertices become opposite rectangle corners.
The straight segment has length √(4²+2²)=2√5 and lies in the unfolded rectangle, so it is a valid surface path.
Every choice of the pair of combined dimensions is congruent in a cube. Other edge-only routes are longer.
The interior space diagonal is shorter, but is forbidden by the surface constraint. The model must preserve where the ant can walk.
hints: Flatten two adjacent faces while preserving distances on each face.
Use a straight segment in the resulting rectangle.
examples.misconception: Use the interior space diagonal.
examples.decision: Explain a feasible unfolding model.

examples.stem: A pyramid is cut parallel to its base halfway from its vertex to the base. What fraction of its volume lies between the cut and the base?
optionRationales: Use linear scaling for volume.
Correct: Derive cubic scaling and subtract the correct region.
Report the removed small pyramid.
Use area scaling.
Square the scale and report the wrong portion.
solution: The small pyramid at the vertex is similar to the original with every length halved.
Its base area is one quarter as large and its height one half as large, so its volume is one eighth.
The region between the cut and base is the remainder, seven eighths.
This derives cubic volume scaling from the area-times-height formula rather than treating the exponent three as a memorized rule.
hints: Identify the similar pyramid at the vertex.
Track both the base area and the height.
examples.misconception: Use linear scaling for volume.
examples.decision: Derive cubic scaling and subtract the correct region.

verification.method: Independent area scale times height scale.

activity.prompt: A cone of height 15 is cut parallel to its base six units from the vertex. What fraction of the volume remains below the cut?
steps: The removed cone has length scale 6/15=2/5 and volume scale 8/125.
The remainder is 1-8/125=117/125.

title: Constrained counting: gaps, exclusions & symmetry
summary: The central question in counting is what one choice represents.
objectives: Construct reversible gap, block, and composition encodings.
Use inclusion–exclusion with explicit feasible intersections.
Handle repeated objects and rotational symmetry without uniform-overcount assumptions.
teaching: The central question in counting is what one choice represents. A good encoding turns each permitted object into exactly one sequence of choices. A bad encoding silently counts some objects twice or gives different objects different numbers of representations.

Before choosing a formula, decide what is distinguishable, whether order matters, and what the constraints forbid. The worked examples establish reversible encodings; the independent problems combine those encodings with exclusions and symmetry.

sections.title: Build a bijection before multiplying
paragraphs: For nonadjacent selected positions, place the unselected objects first and use their gaps. End gaps count. At most one selected object in each gap encodes the separation condition, and removing the selected objects recovers the chosen gaps. This inverse makes the binomial count valid.

For a consecutive block, collapse the block to one object and count the resulting arrangements. Internal order may contribute a factor if the block contains distinct objects; identical letters do not. Divide for repeated objects that remain after the collapse, without dividing again for letters already absorbed into a fixed block.

Stars and bars counts nonnegative compositions into labeled coordinates. Required minimums can be removed by a reversible shift. Indistinguishable boxes are a different problem: sorting the occupancies supplies a canonical representative, while dividing by a fixed factorial can fail when some occupancies are equal.

sections.title: Make the complement and intersections explicit
paragraphs: An at-least-one condition often has a short complement. Mixed committees exclude the all-one-type committees, which are disjoint. Upper bounds on several coordinates produce overlapping violations, so inclusion–exclusion must restore their intersections.

For a cap x≤m, the forbidden shift begins at m+1. After shifting several violating coordinates, check whether the remaining total is nonnegative. This determines which intersections exist and prevents an automatic alternating sum from counting impossible configurations.

A path through a specified point splits uniquely into a prefix and suffix. Multiply their counts because the two pieces can be chosen independently, then subtract from all paths if avoidance is required. The same decomposition principle appears in digit problems, where a leading-zero restriction may affect only one final-digit case.

sections.title: Symmetry changes the size of an orbit
paragraphs: For distinct people around a table, fixing one person removes rotations uniformly. Reflections remain different unless explicitly identified. For repeated colors on a necklace, some colorings have fewer distinct rotations than others, so division by the number of positions is not generally valid.

The fixed-point average counts each rotational orbit once: a coloring with a larger stabilizer has a smaller orbit, and these effects balance. For four beads, count the colorings fixed by each of the four rotations and average. Directly listing canonical rotations provides a small-case check.

Exact-feature conditions need exact exclusions. Choosing one fixed point in a permutation does not make it the only fixed point; the remaining positions must be deranged. Likewise, a geometric feature such as a diameter can count right triangles only after showing that a triangle cannot contain two different counted features.

derivation: Explain the forward and inverse maps for a gap or block encoding.
Write a cap violation as a shifted nonnegative composition and test intersections.
Count fixed colorings under each rotation to compensate for unequal orbit sizes.
pitfall: Dividing by a factorial is justified only when every object has the same number of labeled representations. Equal occupancies and symmetric colorings can break that assumption.

examples.stem: How many nonnegative integer triples sum to 9 with the first coordinate at least 2 and the second at least 3?
optionRationales: Treat the four remaining units as distinct, giving three choices for each.
Subtract one too few from the total.
Ignore the lower bounds.
Correct: Justify a stars-and-bars shift.
Use C(3,2), requiring all three shifted variables to be positive.
solution: Set u=x-2 and v=y-3. The new variables u,v,z are nonnegative and sum to four.
A string of four stars and two bars encodes the triple, so choose the bar positions among six places.
The count is C(6,2)=15. The shift is reversible, so no solutions are added or lost.
If the original variables were required to exceed these bounds strictly, the shift would change. State positivity conventions before applying stars and bars.
hints: Remove the required minimums first.
Count a nonnegative composition of the remaining total.
examples.misconception: Ignore the lower bounds.
examples.decision: Justify a stars-and-bars shift.

examples.stem: How many arrangements of A,A,B,B,C have the two A letters adjacent?
optionRationales: Correct: Prove the block encoding is one-to-one.
Ignore the adjacency restriction.
Count only some forbidden arrangements.
Treat the two B letters as distinct.
Divide again for the A letters inside a fixed block.
solution: Collapse AA to one block X. The four objects X,B,B,C have 4!/2!=12 arrangements.
The division by two accounts for the identical B letters. The A letters have already become one fixed block, so no further division is needed.
Expanding X back to AA gives exactly one original arrangement for each block arrangement.
This explicit inverse is what makes the block count a proof. With a condition involving at least three adjacent letters or overlapping blocks, uniqueness would need a fresh check.
hints: Collapse the required adjacent letters into a block.
Identify which repeated letters remain after the collapse.
examples.misconception: Treat the two B letters as distinct.
examples.decision: Prove the block encoding is one-to-one.

activity.prompt: Count nonnegative triples with x+y+z=8 and x,y,z≤4. Begin with C(10,2) and identify which intersections of cap violations are possible.
steps: A specified violation starts at five, leaving three units and C(5,2)=10 solutions.
Two violations would require at least ten units, so none exist. The count is 45-3·10=15.

title: Double counting, coefficients & cancellation
summary: A combinatorial identity is often one set of objects described in two different ways.
objectives: Interpret weighted binomial sums through marked objects.
Model coefficients as bounded exponent choices.
Prove cancellation and boundary-path counts with reversible maps.
teaching: A combinatorial identity is often one set of objects described in two different ways. Instead of manipulating a long sum immediately, ask what the summand counts, what the index records, and whether the cases partition a simpler whole.

This study develops three representations: marked subsets for weighted sums, local choices for polynomial coefficients, and reversible pairings for cancellations. Each representation turns an algebraic expression into a structure that can be checked.

sections.title: Change the order of counting
paragraphs: A factor k multiplying C(n,k) can mark one member of a selected subset. Choose the subset first and then its mark, or choose the mark first and freely choose other members. A factor k(k-1) marks an ordered pair of distinct members. The distinction between ordered and unordered marks explains a possible factor of two.

Vandermonde’s identity partitions fixed-size selections from two disjoint groups according to how many came from the first group. Binomial symmetry can make an expression such as C(n,k)² fit this pattern. State the containing set and the total selected size before replacing a sum by a single coefficient.

The hockey-stick identity partitions subsets by their largest member. The endpoint shift comes from fixing that largest member and choosing all remaining members below it. This interpretation prevents a memorized identity from acquiring an incorrect upper index.

sections.title: Coefficients encode local choices
paragraphs: In a product of polynomials, choose one term from each factor. The exponents add, and the product of coefficients counts the ways to make that choice. A target coefficient therefore imposes a sum constraint on local exponent choices.

A constant term in a Laurent polynomial is not necessarily absent just because no factor contains a constant. Positive and negative exponents can cancel. Write the total exponent in terms of the number of each type of choice, solve the integer equation, and then count the choices satisfying it.

For factors 1+x+x², each local exponent is bounded. The coefficient of a target power is a bounded composition count, so stars and bars alone overcounts. Inclusion–exclusion removes assignments that choose a forbidden exponent, and direct polynomial multiplication gives a useful independent check.

sections.title: Use reversible cancellation and reflection
paragraphs: Toggling one fixed element pairs even-sized and odd-sized subsets. The toggle is its own inverse and has no fixed points, so the two classes have equal size. With marked elements, toggle an unmarked element to preserve the marks while changing the sign in an alternating sum.

A reflection map can similarly count paths forbidden by a diagonal boundary. Locate the first crossing, reflect only the prefix up to that crossing, and describe how to reverse the map. Reflecting an arbitrary prefix would not establish a bijection.

When a denominator such as k+1 appears in a binomial sum, factorial cancellation may shift the coefficient into the next row. Track both the scale factor and the new endpoints. A missing row endpoint often contributes the small correction that distinguishes the exact finite answer from a tempting nearby value.

derivation: Count committee-chair pairs in both orders to derive kC(n,k)=nC(n-1,k-1).
Partition a selection from two groups by its first-group size to derive Vandermonde.
Toggle a fixed unmarked element to pair opposite signs without changing the counted structure.
pitfall: A suggestive algebraic match is not yet a counting proof. Specify the objects, the cases, and the inverse map so that no object is lost or counted twice.

examples.stem: From eight people, a five-person committee and one chair on that committee are chosen. How many outcomes are possible?
optionRationales: Choose the committee but not the chair.
Allow the chair to be outside the committee.
Correct: Derive a marked-element identity by double counting.
Give the chair an extra binary label.
Choose the wrong number of remaining members.
solution: Choosing the committee first gives C(8,5) choices, followed by five chair choices.
Choosing the chair first gives eight choices, followed by C(7,4) choices of other committee members.
Both procedures count the same objects exactly once, so the common value is 5·56=8·35=280.
The equality is more useful than the numerical answer: it derives kC(n,k)=nC(n-1,k-1), which evaluates weighted sums after the choice order is reversed.
hints: The chair must belong to the selected committee.
Count in both possible orders.
examples.misconception: Choose the committee but not the chair.
examples.decision: Derive a marked-element identity by double counting.

examples.stem: Six objects are chosen from two disjoint groups of five and seven. Evaluate $\sum_k\binom5k\binom7{6-k}$, where impossible choices contribute zero.
optionRationales: Use a containing set of eleven rather than twelve.
Count the two group labels as interchangeable orders.
Count just one split between the groups.
Assume only the first group matters.
Correct: Prove Vandermonde’s identity as an exhaustive partition.
solution: The summand counts selections with exactly k objects from the first group and 6-k from the second.
These cases partition all six-object selections from the twelve-object union.
Therefore the sum is C(12,6)=924.
Including impossible k values as zero makes the notation concise, but does not create new cases. The proof depends on disjoint groups and a fixed total selected size.
hints: Interpret each factor as a choice from one group.
Every six-element selection has a unique value of k.
examples.misconception: Use a containing set of eleven rather than twelve.
examples.decision: Prove Vandermonde’s identity as an exhaustive partition.

activity.prompt: Explain why $\sum_{k=0}^{7}k\binom7k=448$ without adding the eight summands.
steps: The summand counts a k-element subset with one distinguished member.
There are seven choices for that member and independent inclusion choices for the other six.

title: Probability: conditioning, states & expectation
summary: A probability calculation is only as sound as its sample space.
objectives: Construct the correct conditional sample space.
Compress repeated experiments into sufficient states and solve their recurrences.
Use indicator expectations and explicitly specified geometric sampling models.
teaching: A probability calculation is only as sound as its sample space. Conditions can change which outcomes are retained, and repeated processes can require memory of a partial pattern. The productive move is often to replace a large history by a small state that retains exactly what affects the future.

The textbook’s probability-state chapter motivates this approach. Here the state choices are derived explicitly, and finite models are checked by enumeration rather than relying on a plausible-looking fraction.

sections.title: Condition on the information actually given
paragraphs: For a uniform finite experiment, conditional probability can be found by counting favorable outcomes inside the conditioned event. The original denominator is no longer appropriate. Ordered dice or coin strings remain distinct even when the event is described only by a sum or a number of heads.

For a transfer or source-selection experiment, partition into disjoint branches and multiply conditional probabilities along each branch. Add the branches that produce the target event. If the question reverses the information, normalize the relevant joint probability by the total probability of the observed event.

Color patterns are not automatically equally likely when an urn has unequal color counts. Count subsets or ordered selections of distinct balls, or use the correct sequential probabilities. Numerator and denominator must use the same ordering convention.

sections.title: Choose a sufficient state
paragraphs: A state should retain everything that changes the distribution of the next step and discard irrelevant history. For consecutive-head targets, whether the last toss was a head matters; the total number of earlier heads does not. For occupancy parity, actual box counts can be discarded once the parities are known.

Write each transition before solving a recurrence. A two-step update can be simpler than a one-step update when parity alternates the available state types. In the odd-occupancy problem, only one or three boxes can be odd after an odd number of placements, giving a two-state recurrence.

For waiting times, first-step analysis adds one for the next trial and then averages the remaining expectations in the successor states. An absorbing successor contributes zero remaining time. Overlapping patterns require care: a new symbol may preserve partial progress, erase it, or complete the target.

sections.title: Separate probability, expectation, and geometry
paragraphs: Expected counts can be written as sums of indicators. Linearity of expectation requires no independence, so fixed positions in a random permutation can be counted one at a time even though their events are dependent. An expected value need not be the most probable count or even an attainable count.

Collection times can be split into stages with geometric waiting times. At a stage with success probability p, the equation E=1+(1-p)E gives E=1/p. Add the stage expectations after identifying how the success probability changes.

For uniform continuous sampling, probability is a length or area ratio in the specified sample space. Random endpoints, random midpoints, and random lines produce different random-chord models. For cut sticks or intersecting inequalities, draw the joint region rather than multiplying dependent one-dimensional probabilities. Boundary cases of zero area can be excluded for a strict triangle condition without changing the probability.

derivation: Partition an observed event into disjoint joint-probability branches before normalizing.
Write $E_s=1+\sum_t p_{st}E_t$, with zero remaining time in an absorbing state.
Write a count as a sum of indicators and apply expectation linearly.
pitfall: Independence is a property to establish, not a default. Conditioning, sampling without replacement, and competing occupancy parities usually introduce dependence.

examples.stem: A fair coin is tossed until the pattern HT first appears in consecutive tosses. What is the expected number of tosses?
optionRationales: Correct: Choose pattern states and explain their transitions.
Treat nonoverlapping pairs as independent trials.
Use the waiting time for HH, which has different overlap behavior.
Ignore one possible repeated-head delay.
Count only the pattern length.
solution: Let E0 be the remaining expectation before a trailing H is available, and E1 after a trailing H.
From state one, a tail finishes and a head leaves a trailing H, so $E_1=1+E_1/2$ and $E_1=2$.
From state zero, a tail stays there and a head enters state one: $E_0=1+(E_0+E_1)/2$, giving $E_0=4$.
Contrast HH: after a tail from the one-head state, the process loses its partial progress. The different transition, not the pattern length, changes the expectation.
hints: Keep only the suffix that could start the target pattern.
A head after a head still leaves useful partial progress for HT.
examples.misconception: Count only the pattern length.
examples.decision: Choose pattern states and explain their transitions.

examples.stem: A bag contains 4 red and 3 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Given that their colors differ, what is the probability the first is red?
optionRationales: Ignore the condition on the second color.
Normalize by an unrelated color count.
Correct: Use a conditional symmetry with unequal initial proportions.
Report the joint red-blue probability.
Use the initial blue proportion.
solution: The probabilities of the two retained ordered color histories are P(RB)=(4/7)(3/6)=2/7 and P(BR)=(3/7)(4/6)=2/7.
The event of different colors has probability 4/7.
The conditional probability is (2/7)/(4/7)=1/2.
The equality follows from reversing the order of a red-blue pair; it does not require the bag to contain equal numbers of the two colors.
hints: Condition on the two possible ordered color histories.
Compare their joint probabilities before normalizing.
examples.misconception: Ignore the condition on the second color.
examples.decision: Use a conditional symmetry with unequal initial proportions.

activity.prompt: For waiting until HH, complete $E_0=1+(E_0+E_1)/2$ and $E_1=1+\square$. Explain the missing term.
steps: A head from the one-head state completes the target and leaves zero remaining tosses.
A tail occurs with probability one-half and returns to the no-trailing-head state. Solving then gives E0=6.

title: Invariants, pigeonholes & extremal constructions
summary: Some problems ask whether a process can reach a target; others ask for a guarantee or an optimum.
objectives: Discover preserved quantities and distinguish necessity from reachability.
Construct sharp pigeonhole partitions and counterexamples.
Prove extrema with complete bounds, equality analysis, and attaining examples.
teaching: Some problems ask whether a process can reach a target; others ask for a guarantee or an optimum. An invariant can exclude targets, a pigeonhole partition can force a pair, and an extremal argument can bound what is possible. The solution is complete only when its logical direction matches the question.

A necessary condition does not prove reachability. A lower bound does not prove a minimum. The worked examples explicitly pair a forcing argument with a counterexample, and a universal bound with an attaining construction.

sections.title: Find what a move preserves
paragraphs: Compute how one move changes a proposed quantity. Sums, products, parity, residues, and checkerboard color differences are common candidates. If a replacement includes ab+a+b, adding one exposes a product; the useful invariant may be a transformed quantity rather than the visible one.

A sum can identify a unique candidate target while another invariant rules it out. In the three-pile process, all coordinates change by the same residue modulo three, so their pairwise differences are preserved. This information is invisible in the total sum.

An invariant gives a necessary condition for reachability. To show it is sufficient, supply a construction. For adjacent coin flips, a left-to-right procedure fixes each position permanently, and parity forces the last position. This proves that every configuration with the permitted parity is reachable, not merely that forbidden ones are impossible.

sections.title: Choose pigeonholes adapted to the conclusion
paragraphs: Complementary pairs are natural when the target is a fixed sum. Odd-part chains are natural when the target is divisibility. Joint coordinate parities are natural when the target is an integer midpoint. The best partition is derived from the desired conclusion, not chosen because its groups are easy to name.

To prove a least forcing number, show that one more than the number of groups forces the desired event and construct a selection at the previous size that avoids it. Without the avoiding example, the argument gives an upper bound on the threshold but not its exact value.

Residue classes can also support extremal packing. Complementary classes cannot both be represented, while self-complementary classes may permit only one selected element. Their sizes need not be equal when the interval has a partial final block, so count each relevant class carefully.

sections.title: Bounds need equality or a construction
paragraphs: Average arguments are powerful because each object may contribute to several local quantities. The adjacent sums around a circle total twice the sum of its entries. If equality in the average bound would force repeated entries, the bound can be strengthened before a construction is attempted.

An optimization over distinct integers differs from the unrestricted real problem. Balanced repeated values may give an unattainable product. Bound the number of parts, list the feasible patterns, and compare their products. Every case must obey the original distinctness and sum constraints.

A monovariant changes in only one direction and can prove termination. In subtraction-based Euclid, the positive sum decreases while the gcd remains fixed. Pairing an invariant with a monovariant identifies the terminal state and explains why it must eventually be reached. For graph problems, a global count of wins or edges can give a bound; a small cyclic arrangement may attain it.

derivation: Compute the change in a candidate invariant under one legal move.
Build groups in which any two members have the desired relation.
Prove a universal bound, then exhibit and check an admissible equality configuration.
pitfall: Do not promote a necessary condition into a sufficient one. An unchanged sum, a residue match, or an average bound can leave the central existence question unresolved.

examples.stem: What is the least number of lattice points in the plane guaranteeing that some two have a lattice point as their midpoint?
optionRationales: Give the number of parity classes rather than the forcing threshold.
Confuse a possible pair with a guaranteed pair.
Track only one coordinate’s parity.
Overestimate the sharp threshold.
Correct: Design pigeonholes from the desired pair property.
solution: The midpoint coordinates are integers exactly when the two x-coordinates have the same parity and the two y-coordinates have the same parity.
There are four joint parity types: even-even, even-odd, odd-even, and odd-odd. Five points force a repeated type.
Four points need not suffice: the vertices of a unit square have all four types, and no pair has an integer-coordinate midpoint.
The partition was chosen from the desired midpoint condition. An arbitrary division of the plane would not give the needed conclusion.
hints: Translate midpoint integrality into coordinate parity.
Use both coordinates to define the pigeonholes.
examples.misconception: Give the number of parity classes rather than the forcing threshold.
examples.decision: Design pigeonholes from the desired pair property.

verification.method: Four distinct parity classes and a unit-square sharpness witness.

examples.stem: The numbers 1 through 6 are placed around a circle. What is the least possible largest adjacent sum?
optionRationales: Miss a balanced attaining arrangement.
Use the unconstrained largest pair.
Use the average without checking equality.
Correct: Improve a bound by analyzing equality and prove attainability.
Fall below the average.
solution: Each number appears in two adjacent sums, so the six sums have total 42 and average seven.
If every sum were at most seven, they would all equal seven. Two consecutive equations then force the first and third entries equal, contradicting distinctness.
Thus the largest sum is at least eight. The arrangement 1,6,2,5,3,4 attains eight.
The extremal proof has two separate parts: a universal lower bound and an actual arrangement meeting it. Neither part alone establishes the optimum.
hints: Average all adjacent sums.
Investigate the equality case before constructing an arrangement.
examples.misconception: Use the average without checking equality.
examples.decision: Improve a bound by analyzing equality and prove attainability.

verification.method: Independent exhaustive circular arrangements with one position fixed.

activity.prompt: With seven coins in a row, all initially heads, adjacent pairs may be flipped. Is every even-tail configuration reachable? Give a procedure rather than only an invariant.
activity.answer: Yes. Fix the first six positions from left to right; parity then fixes the seventh.
steps: At position i, flip coins i and i+1 exactly when position i disagrees with the target. Earlier positions stay fixed.
Both current and target configurations have even tail parity, so once six positions agree, the last must agree too.

title: Inequalities, equality cases & admissible roots
summary: An inequality gives a bound, but an optimization problem asks whether that bound can occur under the actual constraints.
objectives: Match inequalities to an objective and derive their equality conditions.
Check attainability under interval, positivity, and integer constraints.
Solve transformed equations and inequalities without losing domains or endpoints.
teaching: An inequality gives a bound, but an optimization problem asks whether that bound can occur under the actual constraints. Equality cases, integer restrictions, radical signs, and excluded denominators are therefore central parts of the solution.

This study emphasizes choosing an inequality from the target expression, then checking its equality conditions against every constraint. The same discipline applies when algebraic transformations create candidate roots that may not solve the original equation.

sections.title: Choose the inequality from the structure
paragraphs: A fixed positive sum suggests a product bound, while a fixed positive product suggests a sum bound. The elementary identity (x-y)²≥0 gives (x+y)²≥4xy and exposes equality directly. For reciprocal sums, combine fractions or use Cauchy–Schwarz so that the known sum appears as a factor.

A repeated variable in a product changes the equality proportions. To maximize xy² with x+y fixed, split y into two equal terms before applying three-term AM–GM. Equality then requires x=y/2, not x=y. The number of repeated factors determines the useful weighting.

If a product of positive quantities equals a product of individual lower bounds, every factor must meet its bound. This can force simultaneous equalities and determine a configuration without solving a large polynomial system. Positivity is essential: it makes any strict factor inequality produce a strict product inequality.

sections.title: The domain decides whether equality is available
paragraphs: AM–GM may provide a lower bound attained at a point outside a specified interval. In that case it is a valid bound but not the answer to the minimum problem. Check the interval and compare the expression with an attainable endpoint value, perhaps by factoring the difference.

For integer variables, the continuous equal-variable configuration may be impossible. A local balancing move supplies a discrete proof: moving one unit from a larger positive entry to a smaller one increases their product when the gap is at least two. At an integer maximum, the entries must be as equal as the sum permits.

For sums of distances, equality in the triangle inequality can occur on an entire segment. Do not assume every extremum has a unique equality point. A later condition may select one point from that interval, or exclude the entire equality set.

sections.title: Track equivalence through transformations
paragraphs: Squaring an equation preserves every original solution but can introduce new ones because it forgets signs. State the radical domain and the sign of the other side first, solve the squared equation, and substitute every candidate into the original statement.

For rational inequalities, numerator zeros and denominator zeros both split the number line, but only the denominator zeros are undefined. A strict inequality excludes numerator zeros as well. A sign chart avoids multiplying by an expression whose sign may change.

Floor expressions are controlled by integer and fractional parts. Write x=n+f with 0≤f<1; a small multiple of f has only finitely many floor values. Preserve open and closed endpoints when reconstructing the interval. In polynomial parameter problems, distinct real roots and positive roots are separate demands: combine a strict discriminant condition with Vieta’s sum and product signs.

derivation: Expand (x-y)²≥0 to derive the two-variable product bound and its equality case.
Compare (a+1)(b-1) with ab to prove integer balancing.
Write x=n+f and enumerate the possible floor values of the bounded fractional part.
pitfall: A sharp inequality on a larger domain can be unattainable on the problem’s domain. Verify equality before calling a bound a minimum or maximum.

examples.stem: Positive real numbers a,b satisfy a+b=8. What is the least possible $1/a+1/b$?
optionRationales: Confuse this two-variable constraint with a different three-variable bound.
Use an unbalanced pair without optimization.
Correct: Transform an objective and preserve inequality direction.
Invert the sum.
Report only one reciprocal at equality.
solution: Combine the fractions: 1/a+1/b=(a+b)/(ab)=8/(ab). Minimizing the reciprocal sum therefore means maximizing ab.
The identity (a-b)²≥0 gives ab≤16, with equality at a=b=4.
Thus the target is at least 8/16=1/2, and the equality pair is positive and satisfies the sum.
The direction reverses when passing from a positive denominator to its reciprocal. Writing that step explicitly prevents turning an upper bound on ab into the wrong kind of bound on the target.
hints: Use a common denominator before choosing an inequality.
The numerator is fixed and the denominator is positive.
examples.misconception: Invert the sum.
examples.decision: Transform an objective and preserve inequality direction.

examples.stem: What is the least value of $|x-1|+|x-7|$ over real x?
optionRationales: Try to make both distances zero simultaneously.
Evaluate at a point outside the minimizing interval.
Report the midpoint’s distance to one endpoint.
Double-count the fixed endpoint distance.
Correct: Identify a full equality set in a geometric inequality.
solution: The expression is the sum of distances from x to the points 1 and 7 on a line.
The triangle inequality makes it at least the distance between those endpoints, which is six.
Every x in [1,7] attains six; outside that interval, moving away increases both-distance sum.
Equality need not specify one point. Recording the full minimizing interval is useful when a second constraint is added later.
hints: Interpret the absolute values as distances.
Determine all points lying between the endpoints.
examples.misconception: Try to make both distances zero simultaneously.
examples.decision: Identify a full equality set in a geometric inequality.

verification.method: Piecewise formulas verify the bound on all three intervals.

activity.prompt: For x≥3, AM–GM gives x+4/x≥4. Is four the minimum on this domain? Find and justify the actual minimum.
activity.answer: No. The minimum is $13/3$, attained at x=3.
steps: The AM–GM equality point is x=2, which is excluded.

title: AMC 12: logarithmic & trigonometric transformations
summary: Logarithm and trigonometric equations often become familiar algebra after a carefully chosen substitution.
objectives: Use common-base and exponential substitutions with full domains.
Preserve monotonicity, zero-factor branches, and interval endpoints.
Combine trigonometric identities with geometric or inequality constraints.
teaching: Logarithm and trigonometric equations often become familiar algebra after a carefully chosen substitution. The challenge is to preserve the function’s domain, its monotonicity, and any solutions that could be lost by division.

This AMC 12 study connects change of base, exponential substitutions, symmetric trigonometric expressions, and triangle geometry. The target is usually a transformed quantity, so recovering an angle or every individual function value may be unnecessary.

sections.title: Use one logarithm variable
paragraphs: Logarithms with related bases should first be expressed in a common base. If t=log_b x, then log_(b^m)x=t/m and log_x b=1/t. The reciprocal relation requires x≠1 as well as positive valid bases and arguments.

Combining logarithms into a product can create a polynomial equation, but its roots must satisfy each original argument restriction. The product of two negative arguments may be positive even though neither original logarithm exists. Write the individual positivity conditions before combining.

An exponential polynomial such as b^(2x)+Ab^x+B can be transformed with u=b^x, but u is strictly positive. After solving the polynomial, discard nonpositive candidates and invert the exponential for each remaining one. In nested logarithms, undo functions from the outside inward and check every inner argument.

sections.title: Preserve monotonicity and zero branches
paragraphs: A logarithm with base greater than one is increasing; with base between zero and one it is decreasing. An inequality changes direction when passed through a decreasing function. Keep the positive-argument domain alongside the resulting interval, especially at strict endpoints.

Trigonometric identities should be chosen to match the supplied information. Squaring sinθ+cosθ recovers sinθ cosθ. Combining tanθ and cotθ over a common denominator then uses that product directly. This avoids solving for θ and introduces only the denominator conditions that the original target already requires.

Factor a trigonometric equation before dividing. Dividing sin(2θ)=cosθ by cosθ discards the entire cosθ=0 branch. After factoring, solve every branch on the stated interval, remove duplicate angles, and respect a half-open endpoint such as [0,2π).

sections.title: Connect identities to geometry and bounds
paragraphs: The cosine rule converts two sides and an included angle into the opposite side. The extended sine rule then connects that side to the circumradius. These are useful in sequence: the first recovers the missing chord, and the second uses the chord’s subtended angle.

Angle-addition formulas can produce exact values for angles such as 105° from familiar angles. A multiple-angle ratio may simplify using a squared sine or cosine without needing the sign of the other function, but the denominator must still be nonzero.

A linear combination a sinθ+b cosθ is a dot product between a coefficient vector and a unit vector. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the amplitude √(a²+b²), and the coefficient direction supplies an equality point. Maximizing sine and cosine independently would demand incompatible angles; the unit-circle constraint is what makes the bound correct.

derivation: Derive reciprocal and power-base logarithm relations from change of base.
Expand a squared sine-cosine sum and apply sin²+cos²=1.
Interpret a sinθ+b cosθ as a dot product and verify the amplitude equality point.
pitfall: Algebraic candidates are not automatically function solutions. Check original logarithm arguments, potential zero divisors, and the requested angle interval.

examples.stem: Find the sum of the real solutions of $\log_3x+\log_x3=10/3$.
optionRationales: Negate the second positive solution.
Correct: Explain a reciprocal-logarithm transformation and its domain.
Report the logarithm-variable sum.
Discard the larger admissible solution.
Treat a one-third logarithm as x=3.
solution: The domain is x>0 and x≠1. Set t=log₃x; then t≠0 and change of base makes the other logarithm 1/t.
The equation becomes 3t²-10t+3=0, whose roots are 3 and 1/3.
Undo the substitution to obtain x=27 and the positive cube root of three. Their sum is the answer.
The transformed roots are not the requested x-values. Both original bases and arguments satisfy the domain, so neither candidate is extraneous.
hints: Use one logarithm variable and its reciprocal.
Undo the substitution only after solving the quadratic.
examples.misconception: Report the logarithm-variable sum.
examples.decision: Explain a reciprocal-logarithm transformation and its domain.

verification.method: Exact transformed roots and domain verification.

examples.stem: If sinθ+cosθ=6/5, find sinθ cosθ.
optionRationales: Square the sum incorrectly.
Correct: Choose a symmetric quantity suited to the target.
Halve the square without removing sin²+cos².
Forget the cross-term coefficient two.
Subtract one before squaring.
solution: Square both sides to get sin²θ+cos²θ+2sinθ cosθ=36/25.
The first two terms sum to one, leaving 2sinθ cosθ=11/25.
The product is 11/50. The original value 6/5 lies within the possible sum range [-√2,√2].
For a later target such as tanθ+cotθ, this product would be more useful than finding either trigonometric function separately.
hints: Square the sum and keep the cross term.
Use the Pythagorean identity before isolating the product.
examples.misconception: Halve the square without removing sin²+cos².
examples.decision: Choose a symmetric quantity suited to the target.

verification.method: Independent algebraic identity and feasibility check.

activity.prompt: Solve $\log_{1/3}(x+2)\le-1$ and state the domain before reversing the inequality.
activity.answer: The domain is x>-2, and the solution is x≥1.
steps: The logarithm is decreasing, so its argument must satisfy x+2≥(1/3)^(-1)=3.
The resulting interval x≥1 already meets the original domain.

title: AMC 12: complex geometry & roots of unity
summary: Complex numbers provide both algebra and a plane geometry.
sourceConcept: AMC 12: complex geometry & roots of unity
objectives: Move between rectangular, polar, and polynomial representations.
Use complex multiplication for orientation-sensitive geometry.
Derive roots-of-unity filters and apply them to coefficients and polygon distances.
teaching: Complex numbers provide both algebra and a plane geometry. Addition translates, multiplication rotates and scales, conjugation reflects, and modulus measures distance. Roots of unity connect these geometric operations to polynomial identities and counting filters.

The useful representation depends on the target. Rectangular form is effective for distances and loci; polar form is effective for powers; a root polynomial is effective for symmetric sums and products. Switching forms is often the decisive move.

sections.title: Use conjugation and geometry together
paragraphs: For z=x+iy, the product z·conjugate(z)=x²+y² is the squared modulus. Hence 1/z=conjugate(z)/|z|² when z≠0. On the unit circle, the reciprocal is exactly the conjugate, which turns z+1/z into twice the real part.

A modulus equation |z-a|=|z-b| describes a perpendicular bisector, while |z-c|=r describes a circle. Translate these into coordinates only after identifying the loci. The geometric interpretation predicts the possible number of intersections and helps detect an extraneous algebraic solution.

Multiplication by i is a counterclockwise quarter-turn about the origin. For a different center c, use c+i(z-c). The order of translating, rotating, and translating back matters. For a square, orientation decides which side of a directed edge contains the remaining vertices.

sections.title: Choose polar form for powers and polynomial form for roots
paragraphs: If z=r(cosθ+i sinθ), its nth power has modulus r^n and argument nθ modulo 2π. Track these separately; a correct angle with an incorrect magnitude is still a wrong complex number. Roots of unity have modulus one and equally spaced arguments.

The nth roots of unity are exactly the roots of t^n-1. Vieta gives their total sum, and evaluating the root factorization gives products with a common shift. Excluding the root one replaces this polynomial by 1+t+...+t^(n-1).

Inverse roots can be paired to simplify rational expressions. For a nontrivial root ζ, the pair 1/(1-ζ)+1/(1-ζ^-1) equals one. Check whether any root is its own inverse and whether a denominator vanishes; these endpoint cases determine whether a clean pairing is valid.

sections.title: Filter coefficients and sum geometric quantities
paragraphs: For an mth root ω with exact order m, the average of 1,ω^k,...,ω^((m-1)k) is one if m divides k and zero otherwise. Apply this to each monomial of a polynomial to retain one exponent residue class. The cancellation follows from a finite geometric sum, so no numerical approximation is needed.

Complex walk problems can often return to ordinary counting after real and imaginary displacements are separated. A return to zero requires equal east-west counts and equal north-south counts. Partition by one count, then recognize the resulting binomial identity.

For a regular polygon on the unit circle, a chord from one to ζ has squared length 2-ζ-conjugate(ζ). Summing uses the root sum, while multiplying uses the root polynomial evaluated at one after removing its trivial root. These methods avoid calculating every chord and show why algebraic symmetry can simplify a geometric quantity.

derivation: Multiply by the conjugate to derive the reciprocal identity.
Expand t^n-1 as a product over its roots and evaluate at a chosen shift.
Sum the finite geometric progression of root powers to prove the exponent filter.
pitfall: Modulus and real part are different quantities. Roots on the imaginary axis have positive modulus but zero real part, and strict half-plane conditions exclude them.

examples.stem: Let z=2+3i. Find $z+13/z$.
optionRationales: Replace 13/z by z instead of its conjugate.
Report the real part once.
Subtract the conjugate.
Correct: Explain when a reciprocal becomes a conjugate.
Report the squared modulus.
solution: The relation z·conjugate(z)=|z|²=13 means 13/z=conjugate(z). This avoids a long complex division.
The conjugate is 2-3i, so the sum is four.
If the numerator had not been |z|², the reciprocal would be a different scalar multiple of the conjugate.
The underlying identity 1/z=conjugate(z)/|z|² requires z≠0. On the unit circle it simplifies further to 1/z=conjugate(z).
hints: Compare the numerator with the squared modulus.
Use the conjugate reciprocal identity.
examples.misconception: Subtract the conjugate.
examples.decision: Explain when a reciprocal becomes a conjugate.

examples.stem: Find the sum of the coefficients of $x^k$ in $(1+x)^6$ for k divisible by three.
optionRationales: Assume exact equality among three residue classes.
Correct: Derive a coefficient filter from a geometric-series cancellation.
Keep only the central coefficient.
Sum all coefficients.
Filter parity instead.
solution: Let ω be a nonreal cube root of unity. Since 1+ω+ω²=0, the average [P(1)+P(ω)+P(ω²)]/3 keeps exactly powers divisible by three.
For P(t)=(1+t)^6, P(1)=64. Also 1+ω=-ω² and 1+ω²=-ω, so both other evaluations are one.
The filtered sum is (64+1+1)/3=22.
A direct check gives C(6,0)+C(6,3)+C(6,6)=1+20+1=22. The filter becomes useful when many terms or weighted coefficients are involved.
hints: Average evaluations at the three cube roots of unity.
Check what this average does to a single monomial first.
examples.misconception: Assume exact equality among three residue classes.
examples.decision: Derive a coefficient filter from a geometric-series cancellation.

activity.prompt: For P(t)=(1+t)^8, use P(1),P(-1),P(i),P(-i) to find the sum of coefficients whose exponents are divisible by four.
steps: The four evaluations are 256,0,16,16.
Their average is (256+16+16)/4=72, agreeing with 1+C(8,4)+1.
